title: How Bot Teachers Will Disrupt and Improve Education
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Bauschard argues that AI teaching bots will soon do much of what teachers do and do it better, at least for content instruction in grades 7 and up. He lists what bots can do that teachers cannot, such as starting where each student left off, differentiating at scale, being available at all hours and remaining patient, and acknowledges what they will not do soon, such as organising trips or setting educational goals. He engages the objection that only humans can provide emotional support, countering with cost and uneven teacher quality. His recommendations for schools and leaders include experimenting, raising standards, giving dropouts second chances and recasting teacher certification around coaching. The piece is a confident forecast and advocacy essay rather than an evidence review.
points: Information has long been free, so teachers mattered for teaching content and for social structure; bots threaten the first role.
Bots can start the year where students left off and differentiate beyond what any teacher can.
The social-emotional objection is met with cost arguments and uneven teacher quality.
Teacher roles may shift toward coaching and facilitating individualised learning, not content expertise.
Bot-led courses will likely arrive first in private tutoring outside regulated public schools.
quotes: Information has been widely and either freely or cheaply available for a long time. First, it was accessible in libraries, and now it is available at the click of a button on the internet.
The latter will still be needed, but AI Teaching Bots (AKA Bot Teachers) will soon be able to do a lot of what teachers do and do it better. That’s just a reality.

Imagine the student who got an “A” in algebra but still didn’t demonstrate an understanding of a few key concepts she will need to learn geometry well. A teaching bot can know that and either (re)teach the concept to the student before the school year formally starts or right before they are taught the lesson on the geometric concept the student needs to understand to advance.
This is hard for teachers to hear, but most teachers know they struggle to engage students. This was true before the pandemic, but it got worse after the pandemic.

Teachers will not need to be content experts. While some content knowledge will be useful, especially over the next few years as these systems ramp up, Bot Teachers will know the content as well or better than most teachers.

Tertiary education is incredibly expensive and simply paying for an emotive connection will be a high cost. Similarly, all students cannot afford a human tutor at human labor prices; those that do have a big academic advantage.

One of the core functions of education is transmitting knowledge that exists in paper or electronic form and getting that information into the head of another individual, usually a younger person. This is a multi-trillion dollar industry.
